summary.text: A 21-year-old primigravida woman presented at 15 weeks of gestation with atypical chest pain and severe weakness, with heart rate 98 bpm and blood pressure 110/65 mm Hg. She reported shortness of breath and fatigue since childhood without an identified cause, and an episode of hypotension and syncope in the eighth week of pregnancy that was initially attributed to maternal stress. Her only medications were folic acid and prenatal vitamins.

An ECG was obtained for chest pain, and echocardiography was performed given her history of syncope. It showed retrograde coronary flow into the pulmonary artery, extensive coronary collaterals, marked right coronary artery dilation and the left main coronary artery arising from the main pulmonary artery, confirming ALCAPA syndrome.

She started isosorbide dinitrate and bisoprolol, was advised relative rest and stress minimization, and surgery and CT angiography were deferred until postpartum with weekly cardiology and obstetrics monitoring. At 38 weeks acute hypertension led to hospitalization for preeclampsia evaluation, and an emergency cesarean delivery produced a healthy male infant of 3150 g with an Apgar score of 8.

Two weeks after delivery, CT angiography showed anomalous origin of the left main coronary artery from the pulmonary artery, and she was referred for surgical correction; a Takeuchi procedure repaired the defect. During one year of follow-up her symptoms resolved completely, echocardiography normalized, and an exercise stress test showed no ST-T changes and 10 minutes of exercise without dyspnea or chest pain. The authors call the outcome favorable but the diagnosis delayed.
